cards.#1: The Legacy Leather sits at the top of Sun Mountain’s range and looks less like the rest of the line than anything else they make. Full-grain leather, a single strap, and the silhouette of a bag from before anyone thought to attach legs to one. At $1,200, it is the company quoting its own prehistory back at itself.
cards.#2: The Hometown is twelve-ounce waxed canvas, made for the country’s 250th and capped at 1,776 individually numbered bags. It is the halo product of the current range, and the clearest explanation of why a Montana company keeps leaning this hard on Americana.
cards.#3: Ballistic nylon over fourteen full-length dividers carries more structure than a stand bag usually bothers with. The Matchplay is the best-looking thing in the current line, and the Grove green is the reason why. It is built for people who walk and want their clubs held apart without strapping a cart bag to their back.
cards.#4: The Swift is a Sunday bag built in the Matchplay language. It goes out for the nine holes after work, when carrying a full stand bag is overkill and carrying nothing turns out to be a mistake.
cards.#5: The name carries the history here: the original Eclipse in 1986 was the bag with legs, and the E-2.5 is its lightweight descendant. The invention is still in production and still $224, which makes it the most Sun Mountain purchase in the range.
cards.#6: Sun Mountain built the first waterproof golf bags in 2007, and the E-4.5 is where that line has ended up. Fully waterproof, seam-sealed, and fitted with the VLO leg mechanism, which stands for very low-profile in the company’s own shorthand. At $380 it is the bag for a course where rain is part of the schedule.
cards.#7: Sun Mountain introduced the C-130 in 2005 and it is plausibly the most common cart bag in the game. A 10.5-inch fourteen-way top, thirteen pockets, and an orientation that puts everything facing you once the bag is strapped to a cart. Two decades on, it is still the default answer.
cards.#8: The Matchplay language carries over to a riding bag here, cleaner than the C-130 and considerably more expensive for the privilege. It is made for people who ride and would rather their bag did not read as rental equipment.
cards.#9: This is the C-130 shape cut in the waterproof H2NO fabric, which is the only difference between the two. If the forecast where you play is a variable rather than a formality, it is the version to buy.
cards.#10: The Speed Cart arrived in 1999 as the first three-wheel push cart that folded down properly, and it created a category that had not existed before. The X is the current version of it, and MyGolfSpy made it a staff pick in its 2026 push cart testing.
cards.#11: The PX4 runs four wheels instead of three, which costs a little folded bulk and buys a cart that tracks dead straight across a sidehill. It is the answer if your course is anything other than flat.
cards.#12: The seat clips onto the cart you already own and does nothing else. It is unglamorous and it is $75, and if you walk somewhere with a slow group in front of you most weekends, it is the easiest money in the catalogue to spend.
cards.#13: The ClubGlider runs a set of retractable legs and wheels that take the weight of the bag off your arm entirely, so you tip it and tow it rather than carry it. Sun Mountain launched it in 2008, and travel covers went from a rounding error to roughly seven per cent of the company’s sales.
cards.#14: The Kube is the hard-sided alternative, a clamshell case rather than a soft cover. It is built for anyone who has watched a baggage handler work and would like a rigid shell between that and their driver.
cards.#15: Sun Mountain’s collaboration streak is the most interesting thing about the company’s current era — Victus, Marucci, Realtree, Municipal, Bad Birdie. The limited edition sticks are the prettiest of the small goods the company makes, and at $130 the most decorated way to line up a putt.
cards.#16: The driver cover pairs a canvas body with leather trim and carries no branding to speak of. It is made to sit on top of the Hometown without arguing with it.
cards.#17: The chevron is the dressier of the two covers. It goes with the Legacy Leather bag if you are committing to the whole look, and at $35 it is the cheaper half of that commitment.
cards.#18: The Colter II is a quilted, packable blanket named after John Colter, the trapper who walked out of the Lewis and Clark expedition and into what is now Montana. It is the most Missoula object in the catalogue, and the clearest sign of where the company sits when it is not making bags.

kickers.1: Bags are where the company actually lives. The Eclipse descends from the 1986 bag that started all of this and the Matchplay is the modern flagship, while the C-130 has been the default cart bag since 2005.
kickers.2: Sun Mountain did to walking carts in 1999 what it had done to bags in 1986. The Speed Cart folded down small enough that people actually bought one, and a category appeared where there had not been one.
kickers.3: The ClubGlider is the third Sun Mountain invention here, after the legs and the folding cart: retractable wheels that carry the weight for you through an airport. The Kube is the armoured alternative, a rigid shell instead of a mechanism.
kickers.4: Headcovers, alignment sticks and a blanket named after a mountain man make up the small goods. They are also the place Sun Mountain’s current collaboration habit shows up first.
